what: Insight Enterprises is one of the largest IT solutions providers in the world. It resells hardware and software from vendors such as Microsoft, Dell, HP, Cisco and Apple, and increasingly earns from cloud migration, data and AI consulting, managed services and software licensing advice. More of its software and cloud sales are booked net of the vendor’s cost, which lowers reported revenue but raises margins.
customers: Large enterprises, mid-sized businesses and public sector bodies in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
money: Laptops, servers, networking and devices resold from major vendors.
Licensing, cloud subscriptions and partner incentives, much of it reported net.
Consulting, managed services, cloud migration and AI implementation.
moat: Insight’s moat is scale and relationships: it is among the largest partners of Microsoft and other vendors, holds the certifications and procurement contracts that large organisations require, and can bundle products and services in one contract. Switching away from an established reseller is a hassle for IT departments, but the products themselves are the same everywhere, so margins depend on the services wrapped around them.
risks: Microsoft and other vendors have cut partner incentives for large enterprise agreements, hitting gross profit.
Net income fell from $281M in 2023 to $157M in 2025 under restructuring costs and weaker software profits.
Hardware demand is cyclical and depends on corporate IT budgets.
Debt of $1.5B followed several services acquisitions.
Services growth has to replace declining resale profits, and consulting is a competitive market.
opportunities: Gross margin has risen from about 15% in 2021 to over 21% as the mix shifts to software, cloud and services.
Forward earnings of about 11 times are low if the PC refresh cycle and AI projects lift demand.
The share count fell from 37M to 32M after convertible notes and warrants were settled.
Free cash flow of $274M is about 6% of the market value.
watch: Gross profit growth, the effect of vendor incentive changes, services margins, the hardware refresh cycle and buybacks.
view: Insight looks like a company in decline if you read only the revenue line, which fell from $10.4B in 2022 to $8.2B in 2025. That is misleading. Much of the fall comes from booking software and cloud sales net of the vendor’s cost, which shrinks revenue without hurting profit, and gross margin has risen from 15% to 21% over the same period. Gross profit, the number that matters for a reseller, is roughly flat at about $1.76B.

The real problem is that the profitable part has been squeezed. Microsoft and other vendors have changed partner incentives for large enterprise deals, and Insight has had to restructure, so net income fell to $157M in 2025. The trailing P/E of 27 reflects that depressed base; on forward earnings the stock trades at about 11 times, which assumes recovery. The ttm revenue of $9.0B shows hardware demand is picking up as companies replace ageing PCs.

The investment turns on whether services and AI consulting can grow fast enough to replace the shrinking resale incentives. If they can, Insight is cheap at 11 times forward earnings and a 6% free cash flow yield; if not, it is a value trap with a cyclical hardware business. I lean towards fairly priced with upside: the PC refresh gives near-term help, but I would want two quarters of rising gross profit before calling it a turnaround.
bull: The PC refresh and AI projects lift hardware and services together, gross profit grows again and the forward multiple proves too low.
bear: Vendors keep cutting incentives and services cannot fill the gap, so earnings stay below their 2023 peak.
